Press Releases | Official Website of Reserve Bank of India 

# Press Releases 

 (340 kb)

 Date : Dec 29, 2020

Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India 2019-20

 Today, the Reserve Bank of India released the Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India 2019-20, a statutory publication in compliance with Section 36 (2) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. This Report presents the performance of the banking sector, including co-operative banks, and non-banking financial institutions during 2019-20 and 2020-21 so far. 

 The broad theme of this year’s report is the impact of COVID-19 on banking and non-banking sectors, and the way forward. The highlights of the Report are set out below:

- During 2019-20 and first half of 2020-21, scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) consolidated the gains achieved after the turnaround in 2018-19. 
- SCBs’ gross non-performing assets (GNPA) ratio declined from 9.1 per cent at end-March 2019 to 8.2 per cent at end-March 2020 and further to 7.5 per cent at end-September 2020. 
- Capital to risk weighted assets (CRAR) ratio of SCBs strengthened from 14.3 per cent at end-March 2019 to 14.7 per cent at end-March 2020 and further to 15.8 per cent at end-September 2020, partly aided by recapitalisation of public sector banks and capital raising from the market by both public and private sector banks. 
- Net profits of SCBs turned around in 2019-20 after losses in the previous two years; in H1:2020-21, their financial performance was shored up by the moratorium, standstill in asset classification and ploughing back of dividends. 
- The Reserve Bank undertook an array of policy measures to mitigate the effects of COVID-19; its regulatory ambit was reinforced by legislative amendments, giving it greater powers over co-operative banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), and housing finance companies (HFCs); and it also undertook a series of initiatives to bolster its supervisory framework. 
- The recovery process gained traction with the resolution of large accounts through the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC); the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Securities Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI) channel also aided the process of recovery. 
- The balance sheet growth of Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) moderated in 2019-20 on lower deposit accretion and muted expansion in credit; while their asset quality deteriorated, increased provisioning resulted in net losses. 
- The performance of state co-operative banks improved, both in terms of profitability and asset quality.
- The consolidated balance sheet of NBFCs decelerated in 2019-20 due to near stagnant growth in loans and advances although some improvement became visible in H1:2020-21; notwithstanding a marginal deterioration in asset quality, the NBFC sector remains resilient with strong capital buffers. 
- The Report also offers some perspectives on the evolving outlook for India’s financial sector.

(Yogesh Dayal) Chief General Manager

Press Release: 2020-2021/844

data.report:
# Indian Banking Sector — Performance, Asset Quality and Outlook
## Executive Summary
- The Indian commercial banking sector remained robust during 2023-24 and through H1:2024-25, supported by sustained double-digit balance sheet expansion and strengthening asset quality [S1, S2, S7].
- Consolidated balance sheet growth of scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) reached 15.5 per cent in 2023-24, compared with 12.2 per cent in 2022-23 [S1, S3].
- Aggregate deposit growth accelerated to 13.4 per cent in 2023-24 from 11.0 per cent a year earlier [S1], though it moderated to 9.8 per cent year-on-year by end-September 2025 [S2].
- Bank credit expanded by 16.0 per cent in 2023-24 (excluding merger impacts) [S1] and maintained a steady 11.0 per cent year-on-year growth rate as of end-September 2025 [S2].
- Asset quality reached multi-decadal highs, with the gross non-performing assets (GNPA) ratio declining to a 13-year low of 2.7 per cent at end-March 2024 [S1] and further to 2.1 per cent by end-September 2025 [S7].
- Profitability across SCBs improved for the sixth consecutive year in 2023-24, backed by stable net interest margins and lower provisioning requirements [S1].
## Credit and Deposit Growth
During 2023-24, the consolidated balance sheet of SCBs (excluding regional rural banks) expanded by 15.5 per cent, driven by buoyant bank credit which increased by 16.0 per cent [S1]. Deposit growth also accelerated to 13.4 per cent in 2023-24 from 11.0 per cent a year ago [S1].
[CHART_1]
*Demand deposits for 3 entities across 3 reported periods (2022, 2023, 2024). [S1, S3]*
However, shifting macroeconomic conditions influenced the composition of deposits. Higher term deposit rates—with the weighted average domestic term deposit rate (WADTDR) on fresh deposits of private sector banks rising to 6.6 per cent at end-March 2024 from 4.5 per cent at end-March 2022—drove a faster pace of growth in term deposits relative to current account and savings account (CASA) deposits [S1]. Credit growth remained resilient at 11.0 per cent year-on-year at end-September 2025 [S2]. Personal loans and services continued to lead credit deployment, while industrial credit growth experienced steady acceleration from lower prior-year levels [S2, S9].
[CHART_2]
*Advances growth (YoY) over 2 reported periods (FY24 to FY25) for 1 entity. [S4]*
[CHART_3]
*Slices are the reported term deposits of 2 entities; shares are of their combined total. [S1]*
## Gross and Net NPA Trends
The asset quality of scheduled commercial banks continued a multi-year structural improvement trajectory. The gross non-performing assets (GNPA) ratio dropped to 2.7 per cent at end-March 2024, its lowest level in 13 years [S1].
Asset quality strengthening extended into 2025, with the GNPA ratio declining further to 2.2 per cent at end-March 2025 and 2.1 per cent at end-September 2025 [S7]. Net NPA ratios stabilized at 0.5 per cent at end-March 2025 [S4]. Provision coverage ratios (PCR) remained high at 76.3 per cent, and the half-yearly slippage ratio moderated to 1.4 per cent [S4]. Macro stress tests conducted by the Reserve Bank of India indicate that capital buffers across bank groups remain well above regulatory minimums even under severe simulated macroeconomic shocks [S2].
## Public-Sector vs Private-Sector Bank Performance
Public sector banks (PSBs) and private sector banks (PVBs) exhibit distinct structural dynamics in balance sheet share, credit deployment, and yield profiles. At end-March 2024, the share of PSBs in total SCB assets stood at 55.2 per cent, down from 57.6 per cent at end-March 2023, while the share of PVBs rose from 34.7 per cent to 37.5 per cent [S1]. PSBs continued to account for the majority of deposits (59.3 per cent) and advances (55.5 per cent) within the system [S1].
While PSB credit growth moderated marginally during 2024-25, private sector banks compensated with stronger credit expansion in retail and industrial segments [S2].
## Profitability and Return Metrics
Profitability across the Indian banking sector demonstrated sustained strength, rising for the sixth consecutive year in 2023-24 [S1].
Return on assets (RoA) stood at 1.3 per cent in 2024 and edged up to 1.4 per cent in 2025, while return on equity (RoE) remained firm at 13.6 per cent and 13.5 per cent across the respective periods [S4]. Net interest margins (NIM) moderated slightly from 3.3 per cent to 3.1 per cent as funding costs caught up with lending rate adjustments [S4]. Capital adequacy ratios strengthened further, with the capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) rising from 16.9 per cent to 17.4 per cent, and Tier I CRAR increasing from 14.8 per cent to 15.5 per cent [S4].
> **Data limitation:** the retrieved sources did not provide a period-matched, source-verified series for Profitability and Return Metrics; the figures in this section are cited in the text instead of charted.
## Source-Extracted Quantitative Evidence
The table below surfaces 8 distinct numeric observations extracted from retrieved source text. Values are not imputed; source IDs refer to the report's source list. Search-index extracts are not equivalent to independently fetched publisher pages.
> **Table omitted:** its rows could not be reconciled to directly fetched publisher data with the required labels, periods and values. No values were inferred.
## UPI Transaction Volume and Value Trends
Payment systems in India recorded substantial expansion, led by the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). Technological adoption across scheduled commercial banks advanced steadily, with credit cards increasing to 1,099 lakh units in 2025 (a 7.9 per cent expansion) and debit cards reaching 9,908 lakh units [S4]. Total complaints handled by banking ombudsmen rose to 3,12,204, with 93.1 per cent of complaints successfully addressed or disposed of during the year [S4]. Digital payments infrastructure continued to anchor retail transaction throughput across urban and rural centres.
## Key Risks, Emerging Opportunities and 12-Month Outlook
- **Deposit Competition and Margin Pressures:** Slower deposit growth relative to credit demand has increased competition for term deposits, creating upward pressure on cost of funds and exerting mild compression on net interest margins [S1, S2].
- **Credit Concentration Risks:** While overall asset quality remains strong, rapid expansion in specific retail and unsecured segments requires continued supervisory monitoring by financial institutions [S2, S9].
- **Capital and Liquidity Buffers:** SCBs maintain robust solvency cushions with a system-wide CRAR of 17.4 per cent, well above Basel III regulatory minimums, insulating the sector against potential macroeconomic headwinds [S2, S4].
- **Technology and Cybersecurity Integration:** Accelerated adoption of digital lending, cloud infrastructure, and artificial intelligence necessitates heightened operational resilience and fraud mitigation frameworks across scheduled banks [S5].
- **12-Month Outlook:** The domestic banking sector enters the upcoming period on a sound footing, supported by healthy capitalization, multi-decadal low non-performing assets, and steady credit demand across industrial and retail segments [S2, S7].
